reasons: The tests were read but not run during this review.
The file explains its reasons clearly, which is good evidence of intent.

terms.meaning: how cautious or ambitious the proposed future design is, such as minimal or moderate
a challenge that points out a missing piece, such as an unpriced integration, rather than a wrong citation
a statement the architect makes explicitly about what must be true for the design to work
problems in the current process, such as manual re-typing of data
a pointer to the exact part of the design an objection or assumption is about

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and shared setup
sections.what: Brings in the architect, its payload and objection types, schema types, and the stub client. It also marks the tests as async.
sections.why: Gives the tests what they need without calling a real model.

sections.name: anyio_backend
sections.title: Async runner choice
sections.what: Tells the async test runner to use asyncio.
sections.why: Likely reason: the agent code is written for asyncio.

sections.name: current_state
sections.title: Sample current state
sections.what: Builds a current state with one step and one workflow debt item about manual re-keying.
sections.why: Gives the architect a realistic problem to design against.

sections.name: step
sections.title: Sample architect step
sections.what: Builds one architect step with a sequence number, name, role, description, and citation.
sections.why: Lets tests create steps quickly and vary only the parts they test.

sections.name: output
sections.title: Sample architect output
sections.what: Builds a full architect answer with a purpose, the given steps (or one default), a posture, and a citation.
sections.why: The default answer most tests start from.

sections.name: TestHappyPath
sections.title: Normal architect run
sections.what: Checks a valid run returns an architected future state with the posture kept, uses the standard model tier, and sends the current state and debt to the model.
sections.why: Confirms the normal path and that the architect sees the problem it is solving.

sections.name: TestBoundary
sections.title: Architect boundary
sections.what: Checks the output cannot hold value, saving, headcount, or cost figures, cannot name agents or an exception model, and that steps name a role rather than an agent. It also checks the task forbids value and timelines, returns the architected type rather than a half-filled full state, and lists every posture.
sections.why: Those figures and names belong to later stages, and a half-filled result would look finished when it is not.
sections.watch_out: Adding any of those fields to the architect's output would break the boundary this file exists to hold.

sections.name: TestFailurePaths
sections.title: Architect failure cases
sections.what: Checks duplicate step numbers are rejected, retried once then accepted if fixed, that an unlisted posture cannot be built, that an invented citation is rejected, and that empty evidence still produces a design with empty citations.
sections.why: Duplicate numbers would make the flow ambiguous. Invented citations and invented postures must not get through. Empty evidence should still yield a design.

sections.name: TestStructuralObjectionsMustBeAnswered (part 1)
sections.title: Objections must be answered: part one
sections.what: Explains the purpose of the objection mechanism, then checks that an objection left unanswered is refused, and that an assumption answering a different claim does not count as an answer.
sections.why: A design with no assumptions could otherwise dismiss every objection by saying nothing. Answers must match the claim they are about, not merely sound convincing.
sections.watch_out: Matching is by claim reference, so the references in the objection and in the assumption must be exactly the same.

sections.name: TestStructuralObjectionsMustBeAnswered: test_an_answered_objection_passes_and_the_assumption_survives
sections.title: Answered objections and their rules
sections.what: Checks that an answered objection passes and its assumption is kept with its resolution, that no objections means no requirement, that objections reach the prompt word for word, that every resolution type is offered to the model, and that the prompt refuses reassurance.
sections.why: Stops softened objections and empty reassurance from passing as answers, and keeps the first pass free of a rule meant only for objections.
sections.watch_out: Changing how objections are worded on the way to the model would weaken the whole mechanism.

summary: Tests the future state architect: the design it returns must have clean step numbering and citations, must not carry prices or agent names, and must answer structural objections about its own assumptions.
purpose: Checks the architect's rules, which are to design the flow only, to use roles rather than named agents, and to answer every objection raised against it.
why: The architect is the third stage. Its design must be honest about assumptions it cannot support, and it must not sneak in value figures or agent names that belong elsewhere.
how: Builds a sample current state with one step and one debt item, sample architect steps and outputs, then runs the architect against a stub client. The later tests check that objections are passed through verbatim, that each objection must be answered by an assumption about the same claim, and that the prompt refuses reassurance.
inputs: Sample current state, architect steps, architect outputs, structural objections, and a stub client.
outputs: Pass or fail results. No real model calls.
risks: Objection matching depends on exact claim references, so a changed reference format breaks answers that used to match. Several tests depend on exact prompt wording.
debug: For objection failures, compare the claim reference in the objection and the assumption. For schema failures, check which fields the output class offers. For wording failures, check the task template.
